entry.description: Swaps who did or thought something in reported speech.
entry.childHint: Ask who is doing it and who it is being done to.
entry.approvalNote: Cleared on the printed review pack; returned marked up.

textProvenance.note: Ruled when written; absent from the store until now (R403/R410).
textProvenance.authority: annie-seventyseventh-return.md, read from the file, sha256 1c7070f52f67c5d9664f26f1fdefa17323ff1b9111a84ca7c4d093c8c48f79a7

stem.text: Read lines 22 to 23. What did the elderly rabbit at the gap want from the Mole?

carriers.key: Sixpence for using the private road.

options.value: Sixpence for using the private road.
Help with his own spring-cleaning.
A ride across the river in a boat.
To be let past the hedge himself.
options.execution: It reverses who is passing whom: the Mole is going by, and the rabbit is the one charging for it.

options.value: Some onion sauce for his dinner.

stem.text: Mr Bingley hoped for something on this visit that he did not get. Read lines 5 to 6. What was it?

carriers.key: A look at Mr Bennet's daughters.

options.value: A book from Mr Bennet's library.
A look at Mr Bennet's daughters.
A chance to invite the Bennets to dinner at his own house.
options.execution: It reverses who invites whom: line 9 has the invitation going FROM the Bennets.

options.value: A ride on Mr Bennet's black horse.
A dance with the eldest Miss Bennet.

stem.text: Halfway through the evening, people changed their minds about Mr Darcy. Read lines 30 to 35. What changed them?

carriers.key: The way he behaved, as if he were better than everyone there.

options.value: They found out that he was not really rich after all.
They decided he was less good-looking than Mr Bingley.
options.execution: It reverses line 30, where the ladies declare him HANDSOMER than Mr Bingley.

options.value: The way he behaved, as if he were better than everyone there.
He complained that the ball had ended too early.
Everybody disliked him from the moment he walked in.

stem.text: Read lines 65 to 67. Mr Darcy says Elizabeth 'is tolerable: but not handsome enough to tempt me'. What does 'tolerable' mean here?

carriers.key: Only just good enough to look at.

options.value: Kind, and easy to get along with.
Good at putting up with things without complaining.
Only just good enough to look at.
Very good-looking, so he is paying her a compliment.
Too proud to dance with anybody.
options.execution: Turns the word back on Mr Darcy: it describes Elizabeth, and the pride is his.

stem.text: In lines 20 to 22, what does the stationmaster say Mrs Spencer did at the station?

carriers.key: She came off the train with the girl and left her with him.

options.value: She came off the train with the girl and left her with him.
She waited beside the girl until Matthew came.
She was to bring a boy over from Nova Scotia.
She took the girl into her charge from him.
options.execution: Reverses line 21, where she is the one who gives the girl into his charge.

stem.text: What does Uncle Podger send Jim to Mr Goggles for? (lines 13 and 14)

carriers.key: To borrow his spirit-level.

options.value: To borrow his step-ladder.
To tell him that Pa's leg is better.
options.execution: Swaps whose leg it is: line 13 has Uncle Podger hoping Mr Goggles's leg is better.

options.value: To borrow his spirit-level.
To fetch a bit of picture-cord.

stem.text: What does Aunt Maria say she would like to do next time? (lines 49 to 51)

carriers.key: Go and stay with her mother while the job is done.

options.value: Ask Uncle Podger to let her hang the picture instead.
options.execution: She asks only to be told in time; she never offers to do the job.

options.value: Go and stay with her mother while the job is done.
Send for a man to come and do it properly.
Hide the hammer so he cannot start at all.

stem.text: Look at lines 1 to 3. How does Roberta wake Phyllis?

carriers.key: By pulling her hair, gently but hard enough.

options.value: By pulling her hair, gently but hard enough.
By shouting at her to wake up.
By pulling the blankets off her bed.
Phyllis wakes Roberta by pulling her hair.
options.execution: Line 1 runs the other way round: Roberta is the one who acts.

stem.text: Read lines 15 to 17. What do these lines tell you about the trip?

carriers.key: He kept the trip from his mother.

options.value: His mother would have stopped him going.
He had promised Nan he would go out there.
His mother told him to go round to Ryan's.
options.execution: Line 17 runs the other way: he is the one doing the telling.

options.value: He kept the trip from his mother.

stem.text: Read lines 70 to 81, then lines 86 to 88. What do these two parts together show about the traveller?

carriers.key: He questions her like a stranger, but knew of the governess.

options.value: Jane has met Mr Rochester before, though only once at the hall.
He is annoyed to find her out, and says so.
He questions her like a stranger, but knew of the governess.
Jane is the one who asks, and he is the one who answers.
options.execution: Line 74 runs the other way: he asks, and she answers at line 75.

stem.text: Read lines 5 to 7. What do the squirrels and the rabbits do?

carriers.key: The squirrels peer and the rabbits run away.

options.value: The rabbits peer and the squirrels run away.
options.execution: Lines 5 and 6 run the other way round: squirrels peer, rabbits scud away.

options.value: A pheasant shows its breast deep in the fern.
The squirrels peer and the rabbits run away.
The rabbits run out into the road ahead of them.

stem.text: Read lines 12 to 14. Why is Mrs Umney still working at the house?

carriers.key: Mrs Otis agreed to keep her at Lady Canterville's request.

options.value: Mrs Otis agreed to keep her at Lady Canterville's request.
Lady Canterville agreed to Mrs Otis's earnest request.
options.execution: Line 14 runs the other way: the request is Lady Canterville's.

options.value: She had nowhere else in the world to go after so many years there.
Because she was neatly dressed in black silk.

stem.text: Read lines 17 to 20. What do the family do in the library?

carriers.key: They take off their wraps and sit down to tea.

options.value: They look at the large stained glass window.
Mrs Umney sits down to tea while they wait on her.
options.execution: Line 19 runs the other way: she waited on them.

options.value: They take off their wraps and sit down to tea.
They are shown upstairs to their rooms to change.

stem.text: Read lines 7 to 10. What does Maggie ask, and what does Tom answer?

carriers.key: Whether he will run away tomorrow; he says he will not.

options.value: Whether he will run away tomorrow; he says he will.
Whether he will divide the third jam-puff with her.
Whether he will run away tomorrow; he says he will not.
Tom asks whether Maggie will run away tomorrow.
options.execution: Lines 7 and 8 run the other way: Maggie is the one who asks.

stem.text: Read lines 16 to 19. What is Tom looking forward to?

carriers.key: The pudding, which he knows is to be apricot roll-up.

options.value: The pudding, which he knows is to be apricot roll-up.
The tipsy-cake, which he says will be good the day after.
Maggie tells him what the pudding is to be.
options.execution: Line 18 runs the other way: he says he knows what it is to be.

options.value: He is disappointed that it is not to be tipsy-cake.

stem.text: Read lines 27 to 31. What does Tom tell Maggie to do?

carriers.key: Choose right hand or left with her eyes still shut.

options.value: He says he will give her the jam piece anyway.
Choose right hand or left with her eyes still shut.
Take the half with the jam run out of it.
Maggie tells Tom to shut his own eyes and then choose.
options.execution: Line 27 runs the other way: he asks which she will have.

stem.text: Read lines 43 to 46. What do these lines tell you about Tom?

carriers.key: He finished first and watched her, wanting more.

options.value: He did not know that Maggie was looking across at him.
options.execution: Line 45 runs the other way: Maggie did not know Tom was looking.

options.value: He was pleased to watch her enjoy her half.
He was lost to everything but jam and idleness.
He finished first and watched her, wanting more.

stem.text: Look at lines 53 to 55. Why did Dick not fetch the apple?

carriers.key: Hands broke in and called out for the rum.

options.value: Silver told him to leave the barrel alone.
Dick had seen Jim hiding in the barrel.
Hands broke in and called out for the rum.
Hands told Dick off for sucking at the bilge.
options.execution: Line 55 says John, so the words are aimed at Silver rather than at Dick.

stem.text: Think about the whole passage. How does the writer let us watch Tom work on Ben?

carriers.key: He gives us what Ben can see, but he holds Tom's plan back.

options.value: He hides Ben's mind, but he gives us Tom's all through.
options.execution: Turns the two round: line 12 and line 37 give Ben's mind, and Tom's plan is the thing withheld.

options.value: He tells us the fence had three coats, and then the boys went home.
He shows us Ben giving in first, so the refusals come after that.
He gives us what Ben can see, but he holds Tom's plan back.

stem.text: Look at lines 18 to 21. What does Captain Brown ask to be allowed to do?

carriers.key: Read the company a scene out of the new number.

options.value: Explain that it is a different sort of thing.
Fetch the month's number from his own house.
Make allowances for Miss Jenkyns and her taste.
options.execution: Line 19 has HER making the allowances, so this turns the two round.

options.value: Read the company a scene out of the new number.

stem.text: Look at lines 35 to 37. Why does Captain Brown speak in a low voice?

carriers.key: He meant that Miss Jenkyns was not to hear it.

options.value: He considers it vulgar to publish in numbers.
options.execution: Line 35 gives that opinion to her, and he is arguing against it.

options.value: He wants the whole company to hear the question.
He has begun to lose his temper with her.
He meant that Miss Jenkyns was not to hear it.

stem.text: Look at lines 38 to 42. What does Miss Jenkyns recommend to Boz?

carriers.key: That he take Dr Johnson's style as a model.

options.value: That he take Dr Johnson's style as a model.
That her father take Boz for a model.
options.execution: Line 38 has her father recommending Johnson to her, so this turns the two round.

options.value: That he form his own style upon her letters.
That he stop publishing his work in numbers.

stem.text: Look at lines 10 to 13. What does Mark do when he interrupts?

carriers.key: He keeps the same example and swaps the two boys round.

options.value: He offers to hand Bevis the gun while Bevis shoots.
options.execution: That is the arrangement Bevis gives at lines 10 and 11, put back the way it was.

options.value: He keeps the same example and swaps the two boys round.
He says he might be shooting an elephant.
He wants to stop Bevis before he can finish.

stem.text: Think about the whole passage. How does the writer keep describing Jo’s anger?

carriers.key: The anger is the one acting, but Jo is the one acted on.

options.value: Her hot temper mastered her, and she shook Amy.
The writer tells us Jo is angry, but never shows the anger doing anything.
Jo has her anger under control from the table onwards, and keeps it there.
options.execution: Lines 24 and 28 have it master her and put her beside herself.

options.value: The anger is the one acting, but Jo is the one acted on.
